explanations.explanation: That's the word, baker. The LORD tells Moses the oil is "…to keep the lamps burning continually." (Leviticus 24:2). No off switch, no break. I once spent years in the dark, so a light that never goes out sounds like a dream to me.

Seven days sounds like a nice, tidy number, but it's not what the LORD says. He asks for oil "…to keep the lamps burning continually." (Leviticus 24:2). That means the light keeps going with no end date on it. A week is a good run for a candle, but this is bigger.

A feast is a fair guess, since it's a big occasion. But the LORD doesn't tie the light to one. He asks for oil "…to keep the lamps burning continually." (Leviticus 24:2). No party required. Those lamps are on the whole time.

Evening it is. Aaron tends the lamps "…from evening until morning." (Leviticus 24:3). That's the night shift, baker, and I have respect for anybody who works it. I'd need a very big timer and a lot of coffee.

Midnight is a real hour, but it's not the one the text gives. Aaron tends the lamps "…from evening until morning." (Leviticus 24:3). Evening is where it starts. Midnight is somewhere in the middle of that stretch, baker.

NOON? Baker, at noon the sun is already doing the lamps' job! The text says Aaron tends the lamps "…from evening until morning." (Leviticus 24:3). That's when the light is needed, once the day's gone dark. A lamp at noon is like me setting a timer for a batch that's already out of the oven.

True. The LORD calls it "…a permanent statute for the generations to come." (Leviticus 24:3). So this job isn't just for Aaron's one season. It's meant to carry on down the line. My own edges wore soft over the years, so "permanent" is a big word to me.

This one is actually true. The text says, "This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come." (Leviticus 24:3). So it isn't a short-term gig that wraps up after a season. It's meant to last for the generations. Easy one to second-guess, so no worries.

explanations.answer: On the gold table before the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The loaves are set "…on the table of pure gold before the LORD." (Leviticus 24:6). A gold table for bread. I've never had a counter that nice, and I've baked on a few. Mine had a wobbly leg and a mystery stain.

explanations.answer: On the bronze altar of burnt offering
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd pick a place for offerings, baker, but that's not where these loaves go. The LORD says to set them "…on the table of pure gold before the LORD." (Leviticus 24:6). A gold table, with the loaves in two rows, six per row. That's the spot.

explanations.answer: Inside the ark of the Testimony
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd tuck bread somewhere special, but the ark isn't the spot. The text says the loaves are set "…on the table of pure gold before the LORD." (Leviticus 24:6). The table is where they go, baker, in two rows of six.

Baked just right, and I mean that! "Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD…" (Leviticus 24:8). Week after week, the same day, the bread goes out. No snooze button, no "I'll do it tomorrow." I once had a whole drawer's worth of free time and still couldn't keep a schedule like that.

Once a year would be a very relaxed baking calendar, baker, and I'd sign up in a heartbeat. But the text says "Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD…" (Leviticus 24:8). That's every week, not every year. My kind of schedule it is not.

Every new moon would be a monthly rhythm, but that's not what the text says. It says "Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD…" (Leviticus 24:8). That puts it on the weekly rhythm, baker, not the monthly one.

Israelites, you got it. The bread is set out "…on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant." (Leviticus 24:8). So the bread stands there for them, week after week. And the word "permanent" shows up again, so that's twice in one passage.

Good guess if you're thinking big, but the text is narrower here. The bread is set out "…on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant." (Leviticus 24:8). The passage names the Israelites, so that's who it's for in these verses.

That would be a big crowd, but the text points to a smaller group. The bread "…belongs to Aaron and his sons…" (Leviticus 24:9). They're the ones who eat it, and they do it in a holy place. It's not a community potluck.

Big heart, baker, but the verse names someone else. The bread "…belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place…" (Leviticus 24:9). It's called "…his portion forever." That's Aaron's family at the table, in a holy place. Handing it out to everyone would be like me giving away the whole batch before the first tray cools. I'd mean well, and the box would still be empty.

Close, but this one is false. The text says Aaron and his sons "…are to eat it in a holy place…" (Leviticus 24:9). So the place matters. The verse doesn't say "anywhere they like," baker. It names a holy place.
